about.title: Scotts Valley Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Scotts Valley sits along a busy stretch of SR-17 and hosts a mix of small retail centers, warehouses, and light industrial sites near Glenwood Drive — the kind of workplaces where equipment failures, delivery mishaps, and vehicle-related incidents happen more often than people expect. Santa Cruz County's most recent full-year data logged 16 injury collisions in Scotts Valley, a reminder that roadways connected to job duties, like deliveries or site travel, carry real risk. Under California law, if you're hurt on the job, workers' compensation is typically your primary path regardless of fault. But when a subcontractor, equipment maker, property owner, or another driver contributed to the injury, a separate third-party claim may also be available. LawProactive doesn't practice law — we're a free service that connects injured workers in Scotts Valley with an independent, contingency-fee attorney who can sort out which paths apply to your situation and help you move forward without added financial pressure.

whyChoose.title: Why Scotts Valley Workers Turn to LawProactive

items.title: We Help You Spot the Third-Party Angle
items.desc: Workers' comp usually blocks claims against your employer, but a negligent subcontractor, property owner, or equipment maker can still be held separately liable. An attorney can review your incident to see if that door is open.

items.title: We Understand the Clock Is Ticking
items.desc: California requires reporting a workplace injury to your employer within 30 days, and third-party claims carry a 2-year deadline. Getting matched early helps preserve your options on both fronts.

items.title: We Know Retaliation Concerns Are Real
items.desc: California law prohibits employer retaliation for reporting an injury or filing a claim. An independent attorney can help you understand your protections while you focus on recovery.

items.question: I was hurt driving for work near SR-17 in Scotts Valley — does workers' comp cover that?
items.answer: Generally yes, work-related driving injuries fall under California workers' compensation regardless of fault. However, if another driver caused the crash, you may also have a separate third-party claim against them. An attorney can review the details and explain how both paths might apply.

items.question: Can I sue my employer directly if I'm hurt on the job in Scotts Valley?
items.answer: In most cases, workers' compensation is the exclusive remedy against your employer, meaning a direct lawsuit isn't typically available. That said, if a third party — like a subcontractor or equipment manufacturer — contributed to your injury, a separate claim against them may still be possible. This is worth discussing with an attorney familiar with both systems.

items.question: What if my employer in Scotts Valley discourages me from reporting my injury?
items.answer: California law makes it illegal for an employer to retaliate against you for reporting a workplace injury or filing a claim. You generally have 30 days to report the injury, so don't let pressure from your employer cause you to miss that window. An independent attorney can advise you on your rights if you feel discouraged from reporting.
